quote: 20. INDEMNIFICATION 20.1 Customer shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Vendor from every claim relating in any way to Customer's use of the Services.
rationale: Section 20 contains only a one-way, unlimited Customer indemnity for Vendor covering "every claim relating in any way to Customer's use of the Services", and no Vendor indemnity appears anywhere in the Agreement (Sections 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5 merely presuppose indemnified claims). That is walk-away territory: no Vendor IP indemnity at all plus a one-way Customer indemnity for Vendor's services, so it fails both the fallback and preferred positions. We therefore add Vendor's defence and indemnity for third-party IP infringement, Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused unauthorised access to Customer Data and Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct, with notice, control-of-defence and cooperation mechanics, and narrow Customer's indemnity to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law. Noted but not separately flagged: Section 9.3 cross-refers to remedies "required by Section 20.5", which does not exist in the current draft; if Copperleaf prefers the fallback structure we can instead add the usual exclusions (Customer modifications, combinations, specifications), procure/modify/replace/refund remedies as Section 20.5, and a 3× annual fees super-cap.

verification.notes: All ten preferred elements are met in operative language: the inserted Vendor paragraph carries an express defend/indemnify/hold-harmless duty to Customer and its Affiliates for third-party claims, with the four required trigger limbs (IP infringement of Services or Deliverables, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused unauthorised access to or disclosure of Customer Data, gross negligence or wilful misconduct), plus notice, control-of-defence and reasonable-cooperation mechanics; Section 20.1 is narrowed to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of Applicable Law. The fallback level is incomplete (no modification/combination/specification exclusions, no procure-modify-replace ladder, no refund fallback, no 3\u00d7 annual fees super-cap), but position-completeness is satisfied at the preferred level, so this does not defeat the redline. Minimality holds: the edit inserts the missing Vendor indemnity and rewrites only the one-way Customer indemnity that preferred element 10 requires be narrowed. No survival tail, at-own-expense wording, extra damages categories, or unrelated boilerplate was added; the model language's "including reasonable attorneys' fees" was properly omitted as unnecessary rather than padded in. Intent is preserved: unrelated allocation, remedies and timing survive, and the revision uses existing defined terms (Applicable Law, Services, Deliverables, Customer Data). The dangling reference in Section 9.3 to "the remedies required by Section 20.5" is pre-existing in the draft and is not created by this edit, so it is not an intent failure here. Repair advice if the fallback route is later chosen instead: add as Section 20.5 the usual exclusions (Customer modifications, combinations, Customer-supplied specifications), an express procure-continued-use / modify / replace obligation with a refund of applicable fees if none is commercially reasonable, and an express super-cap of three times the annual Fees on Vendor's indemnity \u2014 which would also cure the Section 9.3 cross-reference.

quote: As between the Parties, Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information, Customer-provided material, and intellectual property Customer owned or developed independently of the Services. No right transfers to Vendor except the limited right to process that material solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer.
rationale: The IP package meets our preferred position. § 14.2 gives us ownership of each Deliverable created specifically for us and contains Vendor's present assignment of all worldwide right, title and interest (plus equivalent assignments from its personnel). § 14.3 confirms Vendor retains only Vendor Technology (defined in § 1.8 as its pre-existing technology, excluding Customer Data and IP we owned before the Effective Date), and routes embedded Vendor Technology to the § 13.2 licence, which is perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free and fully paid, with modification and derivative-work rights for our business. § 14.1 confirms we own all Customer Data and that no right transfers to Vendor beyond a limited right to process it solely to provide, secure, support and improve the Services for us — service delivery, not independent exploitation — reinforced by § 15.1 (processing only on our documented instructions; no sale, advertising, data combination or model training without our express written consent). § 14.4 creates no joint ownership absent a separate signed instrument identifying exploitation rights, and preserves our unrestricted right to use our own feedback. Minor points noted but not flagged: § 14.2 conditions Deliverable ownership on payment of the applicable Fees, and § 15.1 includes an "as permitted by this Agreement" processing hook. Section 13.1's revocable Services licence is a LICENSE-rule issue and is not double-flagged here.

verification.notes: Deviation call is correct: original 21.1 capped both Parties at one month of Fees actually paid (below the 6-month walk-away floor) and the trailing "without exception" neutralised the entire Excluded Claims regime in 21.3, putting indemnities and confidentiality inside an illusory cap. All eleven preferred elements are met in operative language; the level is position-complete, and the fallback is met a fortiori. The edits are confined to the two defective mechanics: (i) the cap basis and the "without exception" override in 21.1, and (ii) the Customer-payment carve-out sentence in 21.3 whose reach was limited by the narrow cl. 1.5 definition of "Fees". Section 21.2, including the Customer-favourable direct-damages sentence, is untouched, and the "undisputed" qualifier is preserved. Enumerating "Fees, taxes, expenses and interest" is close to surplus, but it is required to defeat the cl. 1.5 carve-out from "Fees" and so is tied to the selected element rather than being a free-standing extra; dropping "for conforming Services" is likewise necessary because the element requires coverage of payment obligations as a whole, not a subset. If the drafter wants a tighter edit, "Customer's payment obligations for undisputed amounts due under this Agreement" alone would carry the element. Intent preserved: no dangling terms (Excluded Claims remains defined in 21.3), no contradictory retained sentence, and the mutual damages exclusion, direct-damages characterisation and Order Form fee mechanics survive unchanged. Margin comment accurately states what changed and why and cites the playbook position; tone and prefix conform.

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 meets the preferred position. § 24.1 lets Customer assign to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets without Vendor's consent (notice only). § 24.2 bars Vendor assignment, delegation of material performance, or transfer by change of control without Customer's prior written consent, with the reasonableness standard running in Customer's favour, and bars assignment to a direct Customer competitor. § 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any termination, suspension, repricing, acceleration or service-reduction right on Customer's change of control, so the walk-away trigger is absent. § 13.3 reinforces Customer's licence-transfer right. Only minor wording points fall short of ideal drafting — the competitor bar is qualified by "without Customer's consent" (immaterial, since no Vendor assignment is permitted without our consent at all) and the § 24.2 reasonableness standard omits "conditioned or delayed" (supplied for other assignments in § 24.3). These are noted, not redlined.

elements.evidence: 19.4 (retained): "For breach of Section 19.1 or 19.2, Vendor shall promptly re-perform, repair, or replace the nonconforming item at no charge."

elements.element: Warranty remedies include a refund.
elements.evidence: 19.4: "If Vendor cannot do so within a reasonable period, Customer may terminate the affected item and receive a refund of Fees paid for it."

elements.element: Vendor warrants compliance with applicable laws.
elements.evidence: The rationale asserts Section 19.3 covers Applicable Law, but 19.3 is not reproduced in the cited paragraphs or the rendered operative language, so its scope and party direction cannot be verified here.

elements.element: Vendor warrants that the Services and Deliverables contain no malicious code.
elements.evidence: Same defect: the malicious-code warranty is attributed to Section 19.3, which is not in the record before us; its wording (e.g. whether it covers both Services and Deliverables) cannot be confirmed.

elements.element: Software is warranted to conform to its documentation for at least 90 days.
elements.evidence: Amended 19.2: "For ninety (90) days after delivery or first availability, each Deliverable and any software will materially conform to its documentation." The 15-day period and the post-period remedy cut-off are removed.

elements.element: Services are warranted for at least 30 days.
elements.evidence: 19.1 warrants Services performance and conformity with no stated expiry; with the 19.2 cut-off sentence deleted, no provision terminates the Services warranty before 30 days.

elements.element: Warranty remedies include repair or replacement.
elements.evidence: 19.4: "Vendor shall promptly re-perform, repair, or replace the nonconforming item at no charge", expressly keyed to breaches of 19.1 or 19.2.

elements.element: Warranty remedies include a refund.
elements.evidence: 19.4: "Customer may terminate the affected item and receive a refund of Fees paid for it" where cure fails; the deleted cut-off no longer extinguishes this obligation.

verification.notes: Fallback is complete: the amended 19.2 supplies a 90-day documentation-conformity warranty covering software as well as Deliverables, 19.1 supplies an untimed Services warranty (comfortably above the 30-day floor), and retained 19.4 supplies both repair/replacement and refund remedies keyed to 19.1 and 19.2. Preferred is not reached because the software conformance period is 90 days rather than 12 months, and the compliance-with-laws and no-malicious-code warranties sit in Section 19.3, which is not in the record and so cannot be verified; the drafter correctly declines to press preferred and notes the shortfall in the comment rather than flagging it separately. 'Deviation' is the right status: the original 19.2 gave only fifteen days and expressly ended Vendor's correction and refund obligations thereafter, failing the 90-day fallback floor on a material term. Minimality holds. The three edits — 15 to ninety (90) days, extension to 'any software', and deletion of 'after that date Vendor has no correction or refund obligation' — each map to a checklist element; the deleted cut-off had to go because, read broadly, it extinguished the 19.4 repair/replace and refund remedies that the checklist requires. 'or first availability' is a justified anchor because hosted software under the Services definition is not 'delivered'; it adds no obligation beyond the conformity element and should not be expanded further. Intent preserved: 19.4's cross-references to Sections 19.1 and 19.2 remain valid, 19.3 is untouched, the non-exclusive remedy carve-outs for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims survive, and no retained sentence now contradicts the extended period. Optional hardening if pressed at renegotiation: state the software period as twelve (12) months in 19.2 to reach preferred; no other change is needed.

quote: 18.1 Vendor shall maintain, at its own expense throughout the term and for one year afterward, commercial general liability insurance of at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 aggregate, workers' compensation as required by law, employer's liability of USD 1,000,000, professional errors and omissions insurance of USD 2,000,000, and cyber and privacy liability insurance of USD 5,000,000.
rationale: Section 18 fully meets our preferred insurance position: CGL at USD 1M per occurrence / USD 2M aggregate, E&O at USD 2M, cyber and privacy liability at USD 5M (maintained unconditionally, so it covers Vendor's processing of Customer Data), and workers' compensation as required by law, each for the term plus one year. Section 18.2 requires certificates of insurance on request and confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities. No redline required.
